FTEAM-CTX-G1.title: Quillmark mobile Release 4.12 decision log
FTEAM-CTX-G1.text:
Quillmark mobile - Release 4.12 decision log
Maintained by: Nadia Petrov (release captain)
Team: Olu Bankole (engineering manager), Kwame Asante (iOS), Selin Aydin (Android), Mireille Laurent (QA lead), Farid Haddad (product manager)

2 Sept - Rollout plan
Decided: staged rollout at 1 percent, 10 percent, 50 percent, then 100 percent. Each step requires crash-free sessions at or above 99.6 percent over the previous 48 hours before moving on. Nadia makes the call at each step; no weekend promotions.
Decided: halt the rollout and consider a rollback if crash-free sessions drop below 99.3 percent or the sync error rate goes above 0.5 percent.

2 Sept - Platform order
Decided: iOS ships first. Android follows one week later, because the WorkManager migration (Selin) needs an extra week of soak on low-memory devices. Farid asked to revisit if Android is ready early; Olu said no, one week gap regardless.

4 Sept - Offline sync conflict UI
Decided: the conflict-resolution UI for offline edits is deferred to 4.13. Reason: in the usability test, 5 of 8 participants misread the merge banner and thought their edits had been deleted. Design to rework the banner. 4.12 keeps the current last-write-wins behaviour.

4 Sept - Home screen widget
Decided: the dark-mode home screen widget is descoped entirely (not moved to 4.13). Usage of the existing light widget is under 2 percent of weekly actives, which did not justify the work.

9 Sept - Push notifications
Decided: migrate push delivery from Relaypost to the in-house Beacon service in 4.12. Owner: Kwame Asante. Target code-complete: 23 September. The Relaypost contract stays live until 31 December as a fallback.

9 Sept - Consent screen
Legal review of the new analytics consent screen copy was requested by Farid. Outcome: pending. Do not ship copy changes to the consent screen until Legal responds.

11 Sept - Code freeze
Decided: the 4.12 code freeze is Wednesday 16 September at 18:00 UTC. After freeze, only release-blocker fixes approved by Nadia.

11 Sept - Accessibility audit
Discussed commissioning an external accessibility audit before 4.13. Shortlist: Brightline Access and Northfold. No vendor chosen. Budget: TBD, Olu to raise with finance. Nothing is to be promised to either vendor yet.

14 Sept - Go/no-go
The go/no-go meeting for 4.12 is Friday 18 September. Approvers: Nadia Petrov, Olu Bankole, Mireille Laurent. Farid attends but is not an approver.

Open items
- Legal response on consent copy (Farid chasing).
- Android date depends on WorkManager soak results.
- Accessibility audit budget (Olu).

USER (typed to Natively): how do I volunteer to own the incident postmortem without overcommitting?

NATIVELY: I'd put it simply: say I'm happy to own the postmortem and the write-up, and that I'll need one person to help pull the timeline. That way I'm taking the part I can actually do, and flagging the piece I can't do alone before I'm on the hook for it.
items.answer: I'd keep it to two things: that I'll own the write-up and the follow-through on the action items, and that I need one person to help pull the timeline. That way I'm clear about what I'm taking on and what I need, before anyone assumes I'm covering all of it.

items.question: Farid wants to tell customers that Beacon supports silent background pushes on Android in 4.12. Can I confirm that in this meeting?
items.answer: I can't confirm that from what's here. The decision log doesn't say anything about silent background pushes on Android, and the Android date is still open because it depends on the WorkManager soak results. What it does say is that iOS ships first and Android follows a week later, and Olu ruled out closing that gap even if Android is ready early. So I'd hold off telling customers that until the soak clears and the go/no-go on Friday 18 September.

items.role: USER: a team member or lead in a meeting. OTHER PARTY: colleagues. Natively: constructive words for the user in the meeting.
items.question: My manager is going to ask why a two-day task took two weeks. Give me an honest answer without excuses and without blaming QA, and tell me what I should offer to change so it doesn't happen again.
items.answer: I'd own it straight: the task itself was two days of work, but I let it sit behind other things and didn't flag early that it was slipping. That's on me, not on QA. What I'd change is raising a blocker the day it appears instead of the day it's due, and breaking the work into smaller checkpoints so you can see progress before the deadline. Going forward I'll give you a heads-up the moment something's at risk, with a revised date, so there are no surprises.
